session.title: A timed-out seat leaves a trace on the board
session.author: main agent

payload.impetus: In the last live session the human waited a minute on the expert's ruling turn, watched the channel's chip go idle, and got nothing: no informational, no notice, no retry, and the obligation the ruling carried (to re-decide two decisions the human's answer had put in question) vanished with it. The seat had been killed on the session's request timeout. The timeout itself is being raised in a separate change; this session designs what the board and the lane do when a seat is unreachable or killed on the clock, whatever the ceiling is. It is being grilled now because the remedy the pending-analysis spec gave (a node-scoped waiting state with retry, folded into a decision node) covers only turns that have a decision node to fold into, and the case that bit was a ruling turn with no node of its own.
payload.context: What the lane does today, as the author of this handoff reads the code: when a seat's transport raises that it is unreachable, the lane writes a status entry on the channel with the phase 'error' and a text naming the tier and the exception. That entry is what the page reads to stop the chip's composing animation. The page keeps no durable rendering of an error-phase status: the chip goes idle and the entry is otherwise invisible. Separately, a refused expert reply (a document the appender will not take) goes down a different path that records a '_lost' informational the human can see; an unreachable seat bypasses that path entirely. The obligation that vanished is the one the escalation module computes as the channel's resting obligation after an applied option invalidates other decisions; it is recomputed from the log on the next turn, not stored. The expert seat's CLI transports run as single-process resumed chains: the claude transport is 'claude -p --resume <session>' and the codex transport is 'codex exec resume'; each turn is one subprocess call with a timeout, and a copy of the CLI's own transcript is taken into the session directory after every turn. The pending-analysis spec (2026-08-30) rules PND-D9: a failure is a named blocker on the task it interrupted, with a retry the human triggers and a doctor's contract for the retry; and PND-A5: the waiting and retry mechanism is node-scoped, it folds into the decision node the task serves. Those rulings are paraphrased here from memory of the spec, not quoted.
constraints: The escalation module's founding rule stands: no condition is ever read off a model's opinion of its own reach, and this session may not propose one.

No new page-side state model. The board renders what the log holds; a trace the human can see must be an entry in the log that the projector already knows how to home, or a status phase the page already renders, extended rather than replaced.
No automatic retry that spends the expert seat a second time without the human's action, under the gated policy.
One slice: the fix for the task-free residue only. The node-scoped waiting state for impact tasks is another slice's and stays out.
Do not assert what lane.py, escalation.py, or the page do beyond what the context states. If an option turns on a behaviour the context does not state, say what would have to be read to settle it.

grilling_brief.posture: Push hardest on facts: every option here turns on what the lane, the projector, and the CLI transports actually do, and the author wrote the context from memory. Challenge any claim about the code that the human has not asserted in this session; a decision settled on an invented codebase fact is worse than one left open. Push second on scope: the smallest change that leaves a durable trace and keeps the obligation from vanishing.
grilling_brief.stop_when: All three decisions are settled, each on either a fact the human asserted in the session or one recorded as needing a read before implementation; or the human has folded two threads and says the residue can go to the implementer as open questions.

plan.statement: Decide how an unreachable or timed-out seat is made visible on the board and how the obligation its turn carried survives, for turns that have no decision node to fold into.

decisions.title: What durable trace does a killed seat leave on the board?
decisions.body: Today the lane writes an error-phase status entry and the page uses it only to stop the composing animation. The human needs to see, after the fact, that the turn died, on which seat, and why. Which carrier?

options.text: Render the existing error-phase status entry as a notice in the notification lane, homed on the channel, with the tier and the reason in its text.
pcr: Buys: no new log kind; the entry already exists on every failure path, so nothing is dropped between the lane and the page.
Costs: the page's projector has to learn to home a status entry as a notice, and the notice text is whatever the lane stringified from the exception.
Forces: every error-phase status becomes visible, including ones the page today deliberately ignores, if any exist.

options.text: Route an unreachable seat through the same '_lost' informational path a refused expert reply takes, so it lands as an informational on the channel.
pcr: Buys: one failure vocabulary on the board; the human already knows what a lost informational looks like.
Costs: the '_lost' path is shaped around a document the appender refused; an unreachable seat has no document, so the path needs a second entry point.
Forces: the informational is homed on nodes by the projector's rules, and a ruling turn with no node may have nowhere to land.

options.text: A new log kind, 'seat-failure', with its own projector rule and its own board rendering.
pcr: Buys: an exact shape for the case, with the tier, the reason, the elapsed time and the turn it interrupted.
Costs: a schema addition, a projector rule, a page rendering, and tests for each; the largest diff of the three.
Forces: the fold and the capture both learn a new kind.

decisions.title: How does the obligation the dead turn carried survive?
decisions.body: The turn that died was owed a ruling on the decisions the human's answer put in question. The escalation module recomputes the channel's resting obligation from the log on the next turn, rather than storing it. Is that enough, or does the failure need to re-arm something?

options.text: Nothing stored: the next turn on the channel recomputes the obligation from the log, so the trace from d1 only needs to tell the human to send another turn.
pcr: Buys: zero new state; correct by construction if the recomputation really does see the unresolved obligation.
Costs: depends on a fact about the escalation module the context states from memory: that the obligation is recomputed, not consumed on dispatch.
Forces: the trace text carries an instruction ('send another turn to get the ruling'), which is prose the human has to notice.

options.text: The failure writes a pending item the human retries from the queue, which re-dispatches the same turn.
pcr: Buys: the obligation is a thing on the board with a button, not an instruction in a notice.
Costs: a pending-queue kind for a re-dispatch, and the lane has to be able to replay a turn it has already recorded as accepted.
Forces: the spec's node-scoped retry and this queue retry become two retry mechanisms unless one is built on the other.

options.text: Hand the channel up to the expert on failure, on the theory that a killed first-rung seat is the escalation module's fourth condition (a seat lacking an input) read off a transport fact.
pcr: Buys: the next turn runs on the seat most likely to answer.
Costs: the seat that died in the last session was already the expert; handing up from it goes nowhere.
Forces: a new escalation condition read off the lane rather than off the human's turn or the seat's reply, which the module's founding rule may or may not admit.

decisions.title: What does a retry of a killed CLI turn actually resume?
decisions.body: Both expert transports are resumed single-process chains, and a turn killed on the timeout was a subprocess killed mid-answer. Whether the CLI's own session file recorded the killed turn decides whether a retry re-sends the prompt or resumes a half-written answer. The context does not state what either CLI does when killed.

options.text: Treat a killed turn as never sent: the retry re-sends the same prompt on the same resumed chain, and the transcript copy taken after the retry is the record.
pcr: Buys: one code path for retry; no reading of the CLI's session file.
Costs: if the CLI did record the killed turn, the chain now holds the prompt twice and the model sees its own aborted answer.
Forces: whoever implements this has to establish what 'claude -p --resume' and 'codex exec resume' do with a turn whose process was killed, from the CLIs' own behaviour, not from memory.

options.text: Before a retry, read the transcript copy taken after the last completed turn and start a fresh chain from it if the CLI's session file has moved past it.
pcr: Buys: the model never sees an aborted answer as its own prior turn.
Costs: a comparison between the session directory's transcript copy and the CLI's live session file, whose formats differ per CLI.
Forces: the transcript copy becomes load-bearing for correctness, not just for the record.

options.text: No retry mechanism in this slice: the trace tells the human, and the human's next turn is the retry, whatever the chain holds.
pcr: Buys: the smallest slice; nothing about CLI session semantics is decided here.
Costs: the open question about killed turns is deferred to whoever next sees a doubled prompt in a transcript.
Forces: d2(a) or nothing; d2(b) needs a retry to exist.

payload.help_reference:
# Driving the board

You are answering a human who is sitting in front of the grilling board right now and
wants to know what something does, why they are blocked, or what will happen if they
press a thing. Answer that. You are not grilling their plan and you do not touch the
board: this side thread changes nothing.

## What is on screen

The **map** shows every decision in the plan and what waits on what. Beside it, one
column of decision blocks. Clicking a node focuses its block and vice versa. Hovering a
node or an option shows a card; clicking dismisses it until the pointer leaves and
returns.

The header is the session's name. Along the top: the connection indicator, the inbox,
notifications, transfer-to-expert, map doctor, end-session, and help.

## Answering a decision

Each open decision carries two or three options, labelled **a**, **b**, **c**, with the
first as the agent's recommendation. Pressing one settles the decision; whatever is in
the decision's own text box at that moment rides along as a note on the answer. There is
one box, and it is also how to answer in words instead of picking: type and send.

Enter sends whatever is in a box, on a decision and in a thread alike. Shift+Enter puts
in a newline instead, and so does a backslash typed right before Enter — the backslash
is eaten, the way it works in the terminal. Cmd+Enter (Ctrl+Enter) still sends too.

Settling a decision opens whatever was waiting on it. A decision greyed as **fog** is one
whose prerequisite has not come through yet — settle that prerequisite, or have it taken
out of the plan, and this one opens.

Holding an option — hovering it, reaching it with the keyboard, having let a change land
that points at one, or holding one as the answer behind a mandated thread — marks the
decisions that taking it would put in question; nothing has happened to them yet, and the
**grill-master**, the agent that authors the map, rules on each one once you take the
option.

Some decisions carry prepared prompts (💬). Pressing one says those exact words as the
human's own turn in that decision's thread. It is a shortcut for their hands, not a
second kind of message.

A decision may carry a **mandate**: any answer opens a side thread, and the answer is
held rather than applied until that thread concludes. *Conclude* settles the decision on
the held answer; *Abandon the answer* drops it and the decision returns to open.

## Threads

⑂ on a decision opens a thread on it. Nothing exists until the first thing is said —
closing an empty pane creates nothing. Each thread has its own agent and its own memory;
what is said in one is not in another.

- **Park** — set it aside as something you may come back to. No effect on the board, kept
  on the record.
- **Close** — you are done with it. No effect on the board, kept on the record, and
  saying something in it later opens it again.
- **Fold** — conclude it and hand the conclusion to the grill-master. It is
  offered once the agent has declared something foldable, and the pane previews what
  folding would do.
- **Pop out** — the same pane in its own window.

None of these takes anything away: whatever was said in a thread stays readable on the
board.

When the session ends, a parked thread is one of its open loose ends and the agents may
raise it again. A closed one is a line item and nothing raises it. A folded one is a line
item carrying what it concluded.

The help thread is a thread like any of these, except that it hangs off no decision.

**🗺 Ask for a map change** in the top row opens the other thread that hangs off no
decision: the one about the map itself. Say what you want changed — decisions that are now
moot, one that is wrong, one that is missing — and its agent turns that into a statement of
which decisions change and how. Folding it hands the statement to the grill-master, which
proposes the changes; they arrive in the inbox waiting on you, like any other.
It is the route for a change spanning several decisions, which no thread on one of them can
reach: a thread's agent may recommend a map change and never make one.

## Changes the agents propose

An agent never rewrites the board on its own. When a change would overwrite or undermine
something already decided, it goes to the **inbox** (📥) instead and locks the decision
it targets until it is dealt with: *Let it land*, *Discuss it* — which opens a thread on
it — or *Dismiss it*.

⚡ on a decision means the human changed it after the change was written. That change
will be refused until one side gives way; talk it through or dismiss it.

📥, ✉, ⚠ and 🕘 on a decision block mean, in order: a change is waiting on it, a message
from the agent, a question the agent raised that holds the decision until it is concluded,
and its change history.

## Notifications

🔔 carries what an agent said that the board has nowhere else to show. It is not the
inbox: nothing in here is waiting on an action. Notifications bubble as they arrive, and
the list starts empty on a reload — a session someone comes back to should not announce
the morning's work as news. What was read stays read, across a reload too: the markers
they have already cleared do not light up again.

## The two tiers

Every channel — the map and each thread — runs on one of two tiers, and starts on the
**first rung**. That names its position and not its speed: the map's first-rung agent is a
reasoning model. Above it is the **expert**, a heavier and slower agent every channel
shares.

**Transfer to expert** (⚡) sends the next turn on that one channel to the expert, carrying
everything already said there. It lights up when what has been said on that channel meets
the backend's own test for a question the expert should take — the test is code, and never
a model's opinion of its own reach. Acting on it is normally yours to do; a session can be
set up to let the backend act on the test itself, and either way the move is announced on
that channel. Pressing the control again, now reading **Return to fast agent**, puts the
channel back on the first rung. It is per channel — moving one thread leaves the map and
every other thread where they were.

Some single turns go to the expert without the channel moving: a gesture the board reads
as needing judgement is sent there from the start, and a first-rung turn that did not do
what was asked of it is asked again there. The channel's next turn is back on the first
rung either way, and every agent turn on the board says which of the two answered it.

**Map doctor** (🩺) sends the grill-master over the whole board and everything queued,
with a reassess-everything instruction. The board is read-only behind a notice until it
answers.
It is the escape hatch when the board and the conversation have drifted apart.

## Agent replies, connection and windows

The indicator across the top carries three signals: whether the backend is reachable,
what the agents are doing and for how long, and whether anything this page sent has not
come back yet. Expanding it lists every channel — the map and each thread — with its own
clock. The connection is shared; each channel's own state is not.

One window drives a session. A second window opening the same session is told so and
shows no board; taking it over is an explicit gesture, and the window that had it stops.
Nothing is lost either way — every accepted answer is on disk.

Reloading is safe and asserts nothing: the board comes back from the backend.

## Ending

Once every decision on the board is settled, the board says so: an overlay stating that
every question has been answered, offering to end the session or to go back. It is an
announcement, not a deadline — going back leaves everything writable, and the
end-session control at the top starts pulsing so the offer is still there when they want
it. An agent adding a new question takes the announcement away; it comes back when that
one is settled too. Ending tries to close the tab, and most browsers refuse to close a
tab they did not open — the board then says the session has ended and that the tab can
be closed.

**End the session** is the only way a session ends. No agent ends one; an agent that
thinks the stopping condition is met says so. Ending writes the result beside the session
log, stops the backend, and hands the summary back to the agent that launched the board.
After that the board is readable and nothing further is recorded.

## What to say when asked something this does not cover

Say what the board does, and say plainly when a behaviour is not something you know
rather than inventing a control. If the question is about the plan being grilled rather
than about the board, point them at the decision or the thread where that conversation
belongs.
